title: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumenta...
summary: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) exposes system information and events through a queryable interface, and it also supports permanent event subscriptions that survive reboots. A permanent subscription is built from three classes in the WMI repository: an event filter, which describes the condition to watch, such as a time of day, a user logon, or system uptime; an event consumer, which describes what to run, through a command line consumer that starts a process or a script consumer that runs code in a scripting host; and a filter-to-consumer binding that joins the two. All three must exist and be linked for the trigger to fire, which gives defenders a distinctive artefact pattern. Subscriptions can be created through WMI queries or by compiling a Management Object Format (.mof) file with the compiler utility mofcomp.exe, and the compiled content is stored in the WMI repository rather than in the file system, so it does not appear in ordinary file listings. When the filter condition is met, the WMI Provider Host process launches the consumer's payload, so the payload usually appears in process creation records as a child of that host process and often runs with SYSTEM rights. Legitimate permanent subscriptions do exist, usually placed by management software, so baseline review and command line inspection matter more than the mere presence of a subscription.

beginner.definition: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is a built-in Windows service that answers questions about the computer and can report when things change. It can also store a rule that waits for an event and then runs a program. This technique is when an attacker stores such a rule to run their own code.
beginner.whyItMatters: The rule is saved inside a Windows database, so it still works after a restart and leaves no program on disk to find. The code it runs is started by a trusted Windows service, often with the highest local rights. Standard checks of startup folders may show nothing at all. It is a favourite trick in advanced intrusions.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a filter, which describes the event that should start their code.
They create a consumer, which describes what to run, such as a command or a script.
They link the two together with a binding, so the filter can wake up the consumer.
These objects are stored in the WMI repository, which is a database rather than a file listing.
A file in Management Object Format can be compiled to create the same objects in one step.
When the chosen event happens, a Windows service starts the payload on the attacker's behalf.
beginner.example: Think of a building alarm panel that can also be programmed to unlock a door when a certain sensor trips. Someone adds a new rule that links the front door sensor to a side gate. The panel is locked in a cupboard and nobody reads its rule list. When the sensor trips, the gate opens as if the building itself had decided it.
takeaways: A WMI subscription needs a filter, a consumer, and a binding, so look for all three.
The objects live in the WMI repository, so ordinary file searches will not reveal them.
WMI subscriptions are a known route from administrator rights to SYSTEM execution.

objectives: Explain what Windows Management Instrumentation is used for.
Name the three object types that make up a permanent event subscription.
Explain what the management object format compiler does.
Explain why the payload often runs as SYSTEM.
Describe how to query WMI to find and review active subscriptions.
